objectives: I can use sequence, branching and both count- and condition-controlled iteration in OCR Exam Reference Language.
I can trace a recursive subroutine using stack frames, identify its base case, and compare recursion with iteration.
I can explain scope, distinguish functions from procedures, and predict the effect of passing parameters by value and by reference.
I can describe IDE features that help build and debug code, and apply OOP techniques: encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.

retrieval.q: 2.1.3: what is decomposition, and why does it help a team build a large program?
retrieval.a: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, each solved separately; sub-problems can be shared out, built and tested independently, then combined.

retrieval.q: 2.1.3: what does it mean to identify the order of steps when thinking procedurally?
retrieval.a: Deciding which sub-tasks depend on the results of others, so they must run in a sequence that provides inputs before they are needed.

retrieval.q: 2.1.4: what is a decision point, and which programming construct implements one?
retrieval.a: A point where the route through the program depends on a condition; implemented by selection, e.g. an if or switch statement.

retrieval.q: 1.2.4: state the difference between a class and an object.
retrieval.a: A class is a template defining attributes and methods; an object is a specific instance of that class created at run time.

retrieval.q: 1.2.4: what is inheritance in object-oriented programming?
retrieval.a: A subclass acquiring the attributes and methods of a superclass, modelling an is-a relationship, so common code is written once.

keywords.def: A subroutine that calls itself, with a base case to stop and a general case that moves toward it.
The condition under which a recursive subroutine returns without calling itself again.
The record pushed onto the call stack per call: parameters, local variables and the return address.
The region of a program in which a variable is visible and can be accessed.
Declared outside all subroutines; visible everywhere and alive for the whole run.
Splitting a program into self-contained subroutines that can be written, tested and reused separately.
A subroutine that returns a single value, so a call can sit inside an expression; a procedure returns none.
By value passes a copy, leaving the original unchanged; by reference passes the address, so the original can change.
The same method call behaving differently for objects of different classes, usually through overriding.

content.heading: Sequence and branching
points: Sequence: statements execute one after another, and order matters.
Branching (selection) chooses a path from a condition: if / elseif / else.
switch/case selects cleanly between many discrete values of one variable.
Every program, however complex, is built from sequence, branching and iteration.

content.heading: Count-controlled iteration
points: Repeats a fixed number of times, known before the loop starts.
for ... next manages the counter automatically.
The counter is usable inside the loop, e.g. as an array index.
Use it whenever the number of repetitions is known: process every array element, repeat n times.

content.heading: Condition-controlled iteration
points: Repeats an unknown number of times, until a condition changes.
while tests at the START (pre-conditioned): the body may run zero times.
do ... until tests at the END (post-conditioned): the body always runs at least once.
Post-conditioned loops suit input validation - the user must be asked at least once.
content.note: The while/do-until zero-times distinction is a favourite 2-mark exam discriminator.

content.heading: Recursion
points: A recursive subroutine calls itself.
It needs a base case: a condition that returns without another call.
It needs a general case: a call to itself on a smaller problem, moving toward the base case.
A missing or unreachable base case gives endless calls and a stack overflow.

content.heading: Recursion and the call stack
points: Each call pushes a stack frame: its parameters, local variables and return address.
Frames pop in reverse (LIFO) order as each call returns its value to its caller.
The deepest frame is always the base case; results are combined on the way back up.
Too many frames exhaust stack memory: that is the stack overflow error.

content.heading: Recursion versus iteration
points: Any recursion can be rewritten iteratively, and vice versa.
Recursion: shorter, more natural code for self-similar problems - trees, quicksort, backtracking.
Iteration: one set of variables, no frame per repetition, so less memory and no overflow risk.
Recursion also pays a time cost: every call pushes and pops a frame.

content.heading: Scope: global versus local
points: A local variable is declared inside a subroutine: visible only there, destroyed on exit.
A global is declared in the main program: visible everywhere, alive all run long.
A local with the same name shadows the global - assigning to it leaves the global untouched.
Prefer locals: fewer side effects, memory freed on exit, subroutines stay self-contained and testable.
content.note: In OCR ERL a subroutine writes to a true global only after declaring global inside it.

content.heading: Modularity, functions and procedures
points: Modularity splits a program into subroutines, each doing one job.
Benefits: easier to write, test and debug; reusable; a team can build modules in parallel.
A function returns a single value, so it can sit in an expression: total = double(n) + 1.
A procedure performs a task and returns nothing; its call stands alone as a statement.

content.heading: Parameters: by value and by reference
points: A parameter is the variable in the definition; the argument is the value supplied at the call.
byVal passes a COPY: changes inside the subroutine do not affect the original.
byRef passes the ADDRESS: changes inside the subroutine change the original variable.
byRef avoids copying large data and lets one call send back several changes; byVal is safer.

content.heading: IDE features and OOP techniques
points: Writing: syntax highlighting, autocomplete, auto-indentation and live error diagnostics.
Debugging: breakpoints pause execution; stepping runs a line at a time; watch windows track variables.
OOP: encapsulation keeps attributes private behind public methods, protecting data integrity.
Inheritance shares one superclass implementation; polymorphism lets the same call, e.g. speak(), behave per class via overriding.

worked_examples.title: Tracing factorial(4) on the call stack
steps: The function: if n <= 1 return 1, else return n * factorial(n - 1).
factorial(4): 4 is not <= 1, so push frame (n = 4) and call factorial(3).
factorial(3) pushes (n = 3) and calls factorial(2); factorial(2) pushes (n = 2) and calls factorial(1). Four frames are stacked.
factorial(1): n <= 1 is true - the base case returns 1 with no further call.
Frames pop in LIFO order: factorial(2) returns 2 * 1 = 2; factorial(3) returns 3 * 2 = 6; factorial(4) returns 4 * 6 = 24.
The stack is empty and the final value is 24. Check: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24.
Maximum stack depth was 4 frames - an iterative version would have used one variable throughout.

worked_examples.title: byVal versus byRef: the same procedure, two outcomes
steps: Setup: playerScore = 50, and procedure addBonus(score:byVal) with body score = score + 10, then print inside the procedure.
Call addBonus(playerScore) byVal: a COPY of 50 is passed in.
Inside, the copy becomes 60 and prints 60; the copy is destroyed when the procedure ends.
After the call, playerScore prints 50 - the original was never touched.
Now change the signature to score:byRef and run again: the ADDRESS of playerScore is passed.
Inside, writing score = score + 10 updates memory at that address: 60 prints inside.
After the call, playerScore prints 60. The exam sentence is the consequence: byVal leaves the original unchanged; byRef changes it.

worked_examples.title: Predicting loop output: while versus do until
steps: Code: x = 10; while x > 20: print(x), x = x - 2, endwhile; print("A"); do: print(x), x = x - 2, until x < 6; print("B").
The while loop tests first: 10 > 20 is false, so the body runs ZERO times - nothing prints.
print("A") outputs A.
The do until body runs before any test: prints 10, x becomes 8; 8 < 6 false, loop again.
Prints 8, x becomes 6; 6 < 6 false, loop again. Prints 6, x becomes 4; 4 < 6 true, loop ends.
print("B") outputs B. Full output: A, 10, 8, 6, B.
The trap: assuming the while prints 10 once - a pre-conditioned loop can run zero times; a post-conditioned loop cannot.

activities.title: Russian Dolls and the Tray Stack
instructions: Open a set of nested dolls: each contains a smaller version of the same problem - recursion; the tiny solid doll is the base case. Reassemble to show returns happening in reverse.

Board the factorial function, then give four volunteers a tray each. Student 1 writes n = 4 plus the return address on a sticky note and holds their tray; they cannot answer yet, so Student 2 stacks n = 3 on top, then n = 2, then n = 1.
Student 4 hits the base case: n = 1, announces return 1, and pops off the top.
Unwind: Student 3 computes 2 x 1 = 2 and pops; Student 2 computes 3 x 2 = 6; Student 1 computes 4 x 6 = 24 and shouts the answer.
Ask: what order did trays go on and come off? (LIFO - this pile IS the call stack; each tray is a frame holding a parameter and return address.)
Cross out the base case and ask what happens to the pile. (It grows until the canteen runs out of trays: stack overflow.)
activities.stretch: Trace factorial(0) with base case n == 1: never reached, so it overflows; fix it by changing the base case to n <= 1, then rewrite factorial iteratively and state the memory trade-off.

activities.title: Parson's Problem: The Bouncer's Loop
instructions: Brief: the program must keep asking for an age until it gets 11-18 inclusive, telling the user off after each bad attempt, and must ask at least once. One strip is a red herring.

Strips (shuffled): until age >= 11 AND age <= 18 / age = int(input("Enter age (11-18): ")) / do / print("Thanks, age recorded: " + str(age)) / if age < 11 OR age > 18 then / print("Out of range - try again") / endif / while age >= 11 AND age <= 18 (distractor).
Pairs arrange the strips; before checking, they must trace inputs 9, 25, 14 on a mini-whiteboard.
Correct order: do; input; if out of range then; warning print; endif; until in range; thanks print. Trace output: two warnings, then Thanks, age recorded: 14.
Debrief: why do ... until and not while? Post-conditioned - the body always runs, so the user is always asked; a while would test age before it holds a sensible value.
activities.stretch: Rewrite the validation with while (needs a priming input or a valid flag); which version repeats less code? Then extend it to reject non-numeric input.

activities.title: Sticky Notes versus the Shared Whiteboard
instructions: Write playerScore = 50 on the class whiteboard - this is the variable in memory. Board the procedure addBonus(score) with body score = score + 10.

Round 1, byVal: a volunteer is the subroutine. Copy the value onto a sticky note (score = 50) and hand it over: you got a COPY. They add 10 on the note only (60) and announce inside: 60. At procedure end, theatrically screw up the note and bin it. Class predicts the next print... whiteboard still says 50.

Round 2, byRef: hand the volunteer a note with an ARROW pointing at the whiteboard: you got the address, not a copy. They walk over and change 50 to 60 directly. Bin the arrow note - the whiteboard now says 60.
Everyone writes one sentence per round starting: The original was...
Debrief the exam-worthy phrasing: the mark is the consequence (original unchanged versus original changed), not just that a copy is made.
activities.stretch: When is byRef the better choice despite being less safe? (Large data - no expensive copy; or returning more than one change.) What about addBonus(50), passing a literal by reference? (Nothing to point at - byRef arguments must be variables.)

practice.q: State the difference between a function and a procedure, and give one reason a programmer would choose a function. [2]
practice.a: A function returns a single value; a procedure returns none (1). A function is chosen when the result is needed in an expression, e.g. total = getPrice(item) * qty (1).

practice.q: Explain why a do ... until loop is more appropriate than a while loop for validating user input. [2]
practice.a: do ... until is post-conditioned, so the body always runs at least once - the user is guaranteed to be asked (1); a while loop tests first, so it would test the variable before any input has been entered (1).

practice.q: State the two cases every recursive subroutine must contain, and name the error that occurs if the stopping case is never reached. [3]
practice.a: A base case, which returns without a further recursive call (1), and a general (recursive) case that calls the subroutine on a smaller problem, moving toward the base case (1). If the base case is never reached, calls stack up until memory is exhausted: a stack overflow (1).

practice.q: A function is defined: function sum(n): if n == 0 then return 0 else return n + sum(n - 1). Trace the call sum(3), showing each call and each returned value. [4]
practice.a: sum(3) calls sum(2), which calls sum(1), which calls sum(0) (1). sum(0) hits the base case and returns 0 (1). Returns unwind in LIFO order: sum(1) returns 1 + 0 = 1, sum(2) returns 2 + 1 = 3 (1), and sum(3) returns 3 + 3 = 6, the final answer (1).

practice.q: A global variable count = 20 exists. A procedure assigns count = 7 (without a global declaration) and prints it; afterwards the main program prints count. State both outputs and explain the result. [3]
practice.a: The procedure prints 7 (1); the main program prints 20 (1). The assignment created a local variable that shadows the global inside the procedure, so the global was never changed (1).

practice.q: Given procedure double(n:byRef) with body n = n * 2, and x = 8: state the value of x after double(x), and after the same call if the parameter were n:byVal. [2]
practice.a: byRef: x = 16, because the address of x is passed and the original is updated (1). byVal: x = 8, because only a copy is doubled and then discarded (1).

practice.q: Describe two ways writing a program as a set of subroutines (modularity) benefits a development team. [2]
practice.a: Any two of: modules can be written and tested independently, making errors easier to isolate (1); modules can be shared between team members and developed in parallel (1); tested modules can be reused in other programs, saving time (1).

practice.q: Describe two features of an IDE that help a programmer locate a run-time logic error. [2]
practice.a: Breakpoints pause the program at a chosen line so the state can be inspected (1); stepping plus a variable watch runs one line at a time while showing how variable values change, revealing where they go wrong (1).

misconceptions: Students often assume a while loop always runs at least once; it is pre-conditioned and can run zero times - only do ... until guarantees one pass.
Students often think recursion is free elegance; every call pushes a stack frame, so it costs memory and call overhead, and can overflow where iteration cannot.
Students often say byRef passes the variable's name or value; it passes the memory ADDRESS - and the mark comes from the consequence: the original can be changed.
Students often believe assigning to a name inside a subroutine changes the same-named global; without a global declaration it creates a shadowing local instead.
Students often use function and procedure interchangeably; the defining difference is that a function returns a value and a procedure does not.
exam_link: Command words: write and complete for ERL code (4-8 marks), trace and state the output for loops and recursion (3-6 marks), explain and compare for recursion versus iteration and byVal versus byRef (2-4 marks).
Recursion traces are a 4-6 mark staple: marks sit in the frames pushed, the base case identified, and the returns combined in LIFO order.
Code-writing answers must be OCR Exam Reference Language: endif, endwhile, next i, endfunction all matter for full marks.
Example stem: 'A recursive function mystery(n) is shown. State the value returned by mystery(4) and explain the purpose of the line if n == 0 then return 0.' [4]
task: Write an OCR ERL program that uses a do ... until loop to keep asking for a test mark until it is between 0 and 100 inclusive, printing a warning after each invalid attempt. Then rewrite it with a while loop (you will need a priming input before the loop), and write one sentence stating the behavioural difference between your two versions.
challenge: Write a recursive ERL function power(base, index) that returns base to the power index (base case: index == 0 returns 1; general case: return base * power(base, index - 1)). Trace power(2, 4) showing all five stack frames and the returned values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Then rewrite it with a for loop and give one advantage of each version.

exit_ticket.q: Name the two cases every recursive subroutine needs, and what each one does.
exit_ticket.a: A base case, which returns without calling itself, stopping the recursion; and a general case, which calls itself on a smaller problem moving toward the base case.

exit_ticket.q: One sentence each: what is the consequence of passing byVal, and of passing byRef?
exit_ticket.a: byVal: a copy is changed, so the original variable is unchanged after the call; byRef: the address is passed, so the original variable can be changed.

exit_ticket.q: A global total = 10; a procedure runs total = 5 then print(total); afterwards the main program runs print(total). What prints, and why?
exit_ticket.a: 5 then 10 - the assignment created a local total that shadows the global inside the procedure; the global was never modified.
